record.tranche_reason: Tests superposition and polysemanticity in trained synthetic toy networks, rather than measuring polysemantic neurons in real vision or language models.
record.gate_note: The article mentions InceptionV1 and transformer-neuron findings as motivation or validation, but does not itself measure those real models; those cited or discussed findings are not rows. Results from external comments and follow-up work are also not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: Trains synthetic toy ReLU networks with known ground-truth features. It shows directly that sparse features beyond the dimension count are packed in superposition, yielding polysemantic neurons in privileged-basis models. This is a different method aimed at V3's causal question. It is not one of the original sources (Zoom In, SoLU).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also claim that superposition is governed by a phase change. Features have fractional dimensionalities organized into polytopes. Computation (absolute value) can be done in superposition. Both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons arise, often in the same model, depending on sparsity. They hold that superposition and polysemanticity are likely to generalize to real networks, while the geometry and learning-dynamics results are more uncertain.
record.recipe_differences: Uses synthetic sparse-feature toy networks, learned weights, and representation-geometry analyses rather than the original sources' analyses of real-model neurons.
record.method_sensitivity: Superposition depends on feature sparsity and activation/model setup; the article also reports that L1 regularization and adversarial training can reduce it.

fits_no_version.finding: Vulnerability to analytic L2 adversarial attacks rises sharply (>3x) as superposition forms and tracks features per dimension.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Superposition increases adversarial vulnerability in toy models.

fits_no_version.finding: Superposed features organize into uniform polytopes (digons, triangles, pentagons, tetrahedra), with sticky dimensionalities at 1 and 1/2. Correlated features prefer orthogonal local bases or collapse to principal components.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Geometry of feature superposition in toy models.

record.problems: The evidence is from synthetic toy networks, and the authors explicitly say generalization to real networks is unclear. Several findings are described qualitatively without numeric measurements in the text; for the hidden-layer study, the displayed solutions are selected as the lowest-loss out of 1000 trained models.

untested.parts: No measurements of vision-model neurons. InceptionV1 depth trends are cited as consistency checks only.
No measurements of transformer MLP neurons. The claim that first-layer MLP neurons are extremely polysemantic rests on the authors' experience and is not reported as a result.
Whether superposition explains polysemantic neurons in trained real-world networks is not tested. The authors say generalization is 'very unclear'.

Initialization, regularization or noise as causes when capacity suffices are not tested. Only the n=3, m=6 absolute-value model has enough neurons, and it comes out monosemantic; that is a single case.

SoLU, modern convnets, other activation functions in real models, and performance cost at scale are not tested. The activation-function differences come from Redwood's external comment, not from this study.
No comparison of activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods on measured activations.

missing.what: Linear hidden-layer vs ReLU hidden-layer comparison: with ReLU, features align with neurons and many neurons are dedicated to one feature. This is an activation-function effect on neuron alignment.
missing.locator: Superposition in a Privileged Basis (comparison figure)

missing.what: In the absolute-value model, neurons have a large-weight primary feature plus small-weight secondary features. The authors infer top activations look monosemantic while lower activations are polysemantic. This is inferred from weights, not measured activations.
missing.locator: Computation in Superposition — Superposition vs Sparsity

missing.what: In the absolute-value model at intermediate sparsity, neurons representing the most important features tend to be monosemantic while a subset are highly polysemantic.
missing.locator: Computation in Superposition — Superposition vs Sparsity

missing.what: Adversarial vulnerability rises by >3x as superposition forms.

record.verdict_notes: Rows R1–R5 concern the non-privileged ReLU output model, where 'neurons' are undefined, so they bear on V3's packing mechanism rather than on polysemantic neurons as such. Only R6 and R7 measure neurons. Comment-section results (Redwood on activation functions, Jermyn et al. engineering monosemanticity, which bears on V4 and V5) are external and are correctly excluded. The strategy section argues superposition should be reducible 'a little' with no performance effect; this is argument, not result. Row R4's numbers_found '1/1' is meaningless.

versions.untested_parts: No new measurements of neurons in image classifiers or InceptionV1.
No measurements of MLP neurons in transformer language models or of their share across layers.
Tests sparse-feature superposition in synthetic toy networks, not whether this mechanism explains polysemantic neurons in trained real-world networks.
Does not test whether initialization, regularization, or training noise causes polysemanticity when capacity is sufficient for every feature.
Tests toy-model activation, sparsity, and regularization settings; does not test SoLU, modern convnets, or whether reducing polysemanticity in real models preserves performance.
Does not investigate whether canonical polysemantic neurons in real networks have one shared feature or related offshoots.
Does not compare activation-range sampling or explanation-scoring methods as measurements of polysemanticity.
